Summary: The paper presents a controlled benchmark for LLM writing of knowledge-base entries from exactly the papers the curators cited, built from 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references; 515 papers, 19% readable in full through open access; causal gene withheld). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) writes every draft under six strategies (direct long-context reading, an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence graph, a per-patient case table, recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control) and three add-ons (second-hand passages from later papers, a reconciled case database, a learned curation guide). All strategies share ontology/gene guards and one claim-level audit with a single repair round. The primary endpoint is coverage of fact lists split once, before any draft, from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts over 476 paragraphs); secondary measures cover HPO synopsis terms, allelic variants, causal gene and inheritance. Main findings: hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% (46 entries, 45 better / 0 worse / 1 tied); direct reading, the agentic curator and the evidence graph lie within 0.7 points on the 93 entries all strategies completed and convey 93.6-94.4% of facts the supplied text is judged to state; case table first trails by 1.9 points, mostly on full-text papers; memory-based strategies convey about a third as much; released PaperQA2 and GraphRAG pipelines convey fewer facts at higher cost on 10 and 4 entries, and STORM could not run because the model's safety filter stopped its prompts; planted errors show the audit catches swapped citations and moved sentences but not over-citation, most broadened claims or omissions. All judgements are made by the writer's model family and none was validated by a person.
Strengths: The control is clean. The model, cited papers, guards, audit and scoring are the same for every strategy, and the fact lists are fixed once before any draft, so denominators are identical across strategies (Sec. 3.3). Table 7 shows why this matters: splitting facts afresh for each draft inflates levels by 2-5 points.

The within-paper access manipulation (Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2, Table 24) is a genuine causal experiment with a large and consistent effect: +43.7 points (95% CI +38.3 to +49.1), higher in 45 of 46 entries and tied in one. It is complemented by attributing missed and conveyed facts to the supplied text (Fig. 3, Tables 18-19), e.g. only 1.7% of facts conveyed from abstract-only papers are stated in no supplied text.

Completion is treated as an outcome. Strategies are compared under a symmetric inclusion rule with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis (Tables 6, 12), and App. I.4 documents an earlier asymmetric rule that produced a spurious 2.1-point gap. This is a useful, general lesson for LLM evaluation, where refusals and stopped replies are common.

The statistical reporting is careful and checkable: paired bootstrap intervals, better/worse/tied counts, exact sign tests, Holm adjustment on secondary measures, and separate judge-variation and run-to-run replicate studies (Tables 8-9, 21). The sign-test p-values I recomputed match the paper (e.g. 31/48 gives p = 0.071 in Table 9; 1/9 gives p = 0.021 in Table 34).

The audit stress test (Sec. 4.6, Tables 44-47) gives a concrete, non-obvious finding. Taking the best verdict over cited papers hides over-citation: 0 of 30 added citations were flagged, although the per-paper verdict was 'unsupported' on 176 of 178 such claims. In the real drafts, 4-7% of claim-paper pairs in multi-citation paragraphs are not supported.

The scoping is unusually candid. The paper reports deviations from the design (App. J), null or negative results for all three add-ons (Tables 26-28), a contamination analysis by creation era plus a set of entries created in 2026 (Fig. 5, App. I.2), and an extensive limitations list (Sec. 5).

The benchmark is built only from public resources, and the harness, per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores are released (Reproducibility statement), so other strategies can be scored against the same fixed facts.
Weaknesses: No measurement is validated by a person. The fact splitting, the present/partly/absent judgements, the 'stated in the supplied text' judgements, the audit verdicts and the completeness check all come from the writer's model family (Sec. 3.3; Limitation i). Judge variation (Table 21, 95.7% per-fact agreement between judgings) measures consistency, not validity. For a paper whose main contribution is a benchmark, ICLR reviewers will expect a human-annotated sample with agreement statistics. The gap matters most for Sec. 4.3 / Table 2: the same model judges both whether a fact is 'stated' and whether the draft 'conveyed' it, so errors in the two judgements are likely correlated and the 93.6-94.4% figure on stated facts may partly be an artefact.

Only one model is tested. Every strategy, the audit and every judge use Claude Opus 5.5 (Sec. 3.2, App. B). The central claim, that what the strategy reads limits agreement more than how it reads, may hold only for a strong long-context model on inputs that fit one prompt (median 39,450 characters in the padding entries, Table 38). With weaker, shorter-context or open-weight models, intermediate representations may matter more. Without a second model family the strategy comparison does not generalize, and the abstract and conclusion appropriately restrict it to 'this model'.

The regime tested is one where a null result between strategies is expected, and the regime where they could differ was not completed. Entries have 2-12 references. Padding added only unrelated papers, which every strategy ignored (Sec. 4.5, App. J.2). The large-entry tier yielded no compared entry because of safety-filter stops (Table 43), and the 30-75 reference tier has 10 entries with acknowledged unreliable intervals (App. I.1). The authors acknowledge that the access finding is expected (Sec. 1; end of Sec. 2), so the new knowledge is mainly its effect size in this setting.

The primary endpoint covers a minority of what drafts say. Only about 24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the curator paragraph (Sec. 3.3, App. H). The reference is variant-centred (Limitation ii), and the endpoint is recall-type coverage with half credit for partial presence. Apart from facts contradicted (0.3-0.5%, Table 7), there is no reference-based precision measure, and draft length differs between strategies (97.3-117.9 audited claims per entry among the reading strategies, Table 7), so verbosity is not controlled in the main comparison.

Closeness is asserted but not tested as equivalence. 'Within about a point' (Abstract; Sec. 4.2) rests on intervals that include zero, e.g. the agentic curator at -0.6 (-1.3, +0.0). No equivalence margin, TOST or power analysis is given, while the paper itself shows that measurement choices move differences by about 2 points (Sec. 4.2 'Measurement choices'; App. I.4) and the run-to-run yardstick is +/-1.0 point (App. E). Likewise, on all facts case table first is at -1.9 (-3.1, -0.8) in the main analysis but -1.4 (-4.2, +1.4) under intention to treat (Table 12), with sign-test p = 0.071. The abstract's flat 'trails them' is firmer than the all-facts evidence supports; the deficit on stated facts in full-text papers (-8.4, Table 2; 9/28/3) is the more convincing result and should carry the claim.

The released-system comparison is too small and too modified to carry weight. PaperQA2 ran on 10 entries and GraphRAG on 4 (Table 3; with 4 entries no sign test can reach 0.05). PaperQA2 ran without its agent, and every system used a 384-dimensional local embedder (bge-small) in place of its default, with window averaging (Table 32). The systems answered six concatenated section questions while the strategies wrote an OMIM-style entry in one pass, and only the strategies' drafts were repaired. STORM produced nothing because of safety stops (App. J.1). Indexing a handful of papers per entry for six queries is also the usage pattern that maximizes GraphRAG's relative cost. The text hedges, but putting these results in the abstract and conclusion overstates their weight.

The study depends on one provider's opaque safety filter. Stopped replies remove 7 of the 100 main entries, 10 of the 30 entries created in 2026, every large entry and every STORM run (Table 4), and their reasons are not visible (Sec. 3.2). The missingness may be informative (e.g. by disorder type), and it ties the benchmark's behaviour to one provider's moderation at one point in time. Together with the absence of temperature or seed control through a CLI (Reproducibility statement), this means the comparison cannot be reproduced exactly.

The padding result is summarized selectively. Table 40 shows the strategy-by-size interaction against direct reading at P1 as -2.8 (-4.3, -1.1) for the agentic curator, -3.8 (-7.5, -0.3) for the evidence graph and -4.6 (-7.2, -1.5) for case table first, and direct reading's own gain as +3.6 (+1.0, +5.9). Sec. 4.5 says no strategy lost more than about a point and treats direct reading's rise as noise. With 6 entries neither reading is reliable, but the main text should present both.

Reading and recall are not cleanly separated. Within abstract-only papers, direct-reading coverage falls from 49.8% in the 600000-609999 band to 37.9% in the newest band (Sec. 4.2; Table 16), and the memory-only control conveys 24.1% in that band (Table 17). The reference text itself (OMIM descriptions in ClinVar) is public and plausibly in pretraining data. The 2026 set helps but is small (20 compared entries, five strategies, App. I.2).

The presentation is very dense. The main text packs about 15 experiments into 10 pages, with heavy hedging and many pointers to 47 appendix tables. The paper never shows an example entry, a fixed fact list, a draft paragraph with its audit, or the strategy and judge prompts. Several side experiments (padding on 6 entries, large entries with 0 compared, qualifier deletions with 2-8 items per rule) dilute the focus without changing the conclusions.

There is little methodological novelty for ICLR. The strategies re-implement known paradigms, the learned guide is a small reflection-based prompt with no clear held-out effect (+1.0, +0.0 to +2.0, Table 28), and no new method or learning insight is proposed. Relevance to the ICLR audience therefore rests on the measurement lessons (Sec. 5), which would be stronger if tested beyond one curated knowledge base and one model.
Questions: Can you add a human validation study on a random sample of (a) fact splits (atomicity and faithfulness to the paragraph), (b) present/partly/absent judgements, (c) 'stated in the supplied text' judgements and (d) audit verdicts, reporting agreement with the model judge? Even 200-300 items would materially strengthen Tables 1-2.

Can you run at least direct reading and the evidence graph with a different model family as writer (ideally an open-weight long-context model), and a different family as judge, on the 93 compared entries? Does the access-versus-strategy conclusion survive?

What difference in OMIM facts conveyed would you consider practically negligible, and do equivalence tests (TOST) at that margin support the 'close' claim for the agentic curator and the evidence graph?
How sensitive are the paired differences to the half credit for 'partly present'? Table 7 reports levels with no partial credit; can the corresponding paired differences be added to Table 8?

Is there any pattern in which entries or papers the safety filter stopped (disorder category, content about minors, prenatal or reproductive topics)? Does the access effect or the strategy ranking change when the analysis is restricted to entries with no stopped call in any condition?
How do you reconcile the negative P1 interactions in Table 40 with the summary in Sec. 4.5 that padding cost no strategy more than about a point?
Can you report a reference-anchored precision measure, or coverage normalized by draft length, so that verbosity is controlled across strategies?

For the released systems, how much does replacing the default embedding model with bge-small-en-v1.5 change PaperQA2's retrieval? Was a stronger embedder tried, and can GraphRAG be run on more entries?
Can the qualifier-deletion classes (2-8 items per rule, Table 45) be scaled up so that the claim that the audit misses most broadened claims rests on more than a handful of items per rule?
Will the fact-list identifiers, the prompts and the reply cache be released, so that new strategies can be scored against exactly the same denominators and judges?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section (Sec. 5, items i-xi) is thorough and candid, and the ethics statement correctly says that drafts are not clinical guidance and must be marked as machine generated.

Not discussed enough: completion and the large-entry results depend on one provider's opaque, time-varying safety filter, so they are specific to that provider and that point in time and may not transfer to other models.
Not discussed enough: the reference text is public (OMIM descriptions in ClinVar) and may itself be memorized; the creation-era analysis and the 20-entry 2026 set address this only partly.
Costs are list prices for one model, and GraphRAG's per-entry indexing over a few papers is charged in full, so the cost comparison does not carry over to other deployment patterns.

Because the curator text cannot be redistributed, third parties must rebuild the reference. The paper should state the exact rebuild procedure and its versioning so the benchmark stays usable as ClinVar changes.
